newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end down after bounce on Fed report.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end down after bounce on Fed report.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended lower on Wednesday after scoring a short-lived bounce on the Federal Reserve's milder-than-expected anecdotal account of business and economic conditions around the nation.

Corporate supply weighed on an otherwise featureless trading session until mid-afternoon when the Fed released its so-called Beige Book report, traders said. Investors are worried the Fed's perception of a tight labor market and potentially inflationary wage pressures will cause Fed policy makers to raise interest rates as soon as March 25.
With that in mind, the market was attuned to Beige Book descriptions of the labor market and its capacity to produce higher wages and eventually, higher prices.
When the Beige Book summarized price pressures as temperate and wage gains as moderate despite the tight job market, investors breathed a sigh of relief.
Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc., said the Beige Book's full text delineated "a lot of strong elements" in the U.S. economy.
Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A., said in a day devoid of many events, the Beige Book offered nothing that was startling.

"It read like past reports where we had moderate growth and low inflation," he said. "The market tried to bounce on that but it turned out buyers are still very cautious ahead of the (February) retail sales number -- and with good reason."

Stiles said if the February retail sales data, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Thursday, are strong, "a lot of people will see them as tipping the scales toward a March 25 (Federal Reserve interest-rate) tightening."
Stiles said many people are confused about whether the Fed will raise rates in March or wait until May and Fed officials, themselves, sometimes appear as if they are undecided.
"With that kind of (influential) data looming, it was just impossible to get prices going higher on a fairly acceptable Beige Book report," said Stiles.
"The market was nervous about the upcoming retail sales numbers," agreed Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Inc.

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that retail sales rose 0.6 percent in February and 0.7 percent when auto sales were excluded. In January, sales rose 0.6 percent and just 0.4 percent when auto sales were deleted.
The benchmark 30-year bond ended at 96-24/32, down 11/32 to yield 6.88 percent.
Three-month bill rates ended two basis points higher at 5.06 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.18 percent. Year bill rates were unchanged at 5.38 percent.
Two-year notes slipped 2/32 at 99-18/32, yielding 6.11 percent. Five-year notes were down 3/32 at 99-6/32, yielding 6.44 percent. Ten-year notes were down 6/32 to 97-13/32, yielding 6.61 percent.
